Script leans NE. As a 8-point favorite they project to lead much of the game, tilting toward the run late — Rhamondre Stevenson's carry ceiling rises in the blowout branches. Meanwhile LV throw to keep pace, a volume tailwind for Tre Tucker.

The NE host the LV as favorites of 8.5, with the total set at 44.5 — a market that implies a NE 26–18 scoreline. Running the game forward from that baseline, we expect a contest that spends roughly 39% of its snaps with NE in front, 35% within one score, and 26% with NE chasing. That distribution is the engine of everything below: game state is what turns a team's tendencies into a specific player's workload, so before we get to individuals it's worth being explicit about how this game is likely to be played.

This projects as a game NE should control. A favorite of 8 sits in front for the majority of the second half in most simulations, which pulls the script toward the run and clock management for NE and toward volume passing and tempo for LV, who will be throwing to keep pace. Expect LV to run more total plays than NE — trailing teams go no-huddle (league no-huddle rate climbs from ~8% in neutral game states to over 20% when down two scores), and that extra volume is a tailwind for LV's pass-catchers even in a losing effort.

The Key Matchups

Drake Maye adds rushing value — he scrambles on 5.8% of dropbacks, live for rush-yard and anytime-TD props.

Tre Tucker faces a tough cover — NE hold WR1s to just 50 yds/game (vs ~58); a rec-yards under lean.

Touchdown Board

Hunter Henry is a live anytime-TD dart — LV are leaky to tight ends in the end zone (0.32 TE TDs/game vs ~0.24).

A.J. Brown carries TD equity — LV surrender 0.44 WR1 receiving scores a game.

In the red zone LV throw it (59% pass inside the 20) — Tre Tucker's TD equity over a goal-line back.

Game Script, Pace & Environment

A middling 44 total — no strong lean either way; the value is in the individual matchups above, not the game environment.

NE — a run-heavy offense

NE are one of the league's more run-committed offenses: on early downs while leading, they pass just 39% of the time, against a league average of 44% — a genuine clock-bleeding identity, not noise (it holds after shrinking their sample toward the league).

This is the profile that most rewards a lead back. As a 8-point favorite projected to lead for 39% of snaps, NE will be running to close the game, and their run-first identity compounds it. Rhamondre Stevenson is the beneficiary — we project 14 carries for 60 yards, and his ceiling is where the value sits: in the simulations where this becomes a two-score game, his volume spikes as NE salt it away.

The flip side: A.J. Brown (7 targets, 70 yards) has his ceiling capped by the same script that helps the run game — when NE lead and run, there simply aren't as many pass attempts to go around. He's a safer floor than ceiling play in this spot.

Underneath, Hunter Henry (TE, 5 targets, 37 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

LV — a balanced offense

LV are a balanced offense — their run/pass split by game state tracks the league closely (46% pass when leading vs 44% average), so their players' usage is driven more by role than by any strong situational lean.

Game script works against the run here — LV project to trail and throw, which squeezes Ashton Jeanty's rushing projection (17 carries, 63 yards) but raises his value as a receiver; trailing teams check the ball down, and his target share ticks up as the game gets away from them.

Tre Tucker is the one to target from a volume standpoint: as underdogs throwing to keep pace, LV funnel work to their top receiver — 6 targets for 46 yards projected, with genuine upside if they fall behind early and the game turns one-dimensional.

Underneath, Brock Bowers (TE, 6 targets, 51 yards) is the dependable secondary read — and note the red zone stays TE-friendly regardless of score, so his touchdown equity holds up even if the game script shifts.

What to watch

The single biggest swing factor is availability — use the injury tool in the sidebar to mark anyone out; a starter's absence doesn't just remove his line, it redistributes his targets and carries to specific teammates, and the report and projections rebuild around it. Beyond that: if this game breaks toward the projected 8-point margin, the garbage-time backups (the ◆-flagged rows below) are where soft lines and real edge tend to appear — those depth players get fed in blowouts, and the market is slowest to price them.

This preview and the projections below regenerate through the week as injuries, weather and line moves update the inputs.
